approved: Education Legislation Amendment (Up-front Payments Tuition Protection) Bill 2020
Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
This bill would extend the Australian Government's Tuition Protection Service to cover domestic students who pay their higher education fees up-front at private providers.

It would rename existing bodies and funds to cover both up-front and HELP-assisted students, require private providers to pay annual levies based on their size and risk, and impose new registration conditions and obligations on providers in case of default.
The new arrangements would start on 1 January 2021 and would not apply to public universities, TAFEs, or government-funded providers.

Renames the 'HELP Tuition Protection Director' to 'Higher Education Tuition Protection Director' and the 'HELP Tuition Protection Fund Advisory Board' to 'Higher Education Tuition Protection Fund Advisory Board'.
Requires private higher education providers to contribute annual levies under the Levy Bill.
Imposes a new condition of registration on providers to comply with tuition protection requirements, including record-keeping and information provision.
Allows the Minister to make Up-front Payments Guidelines.
Provides affected students with a choice between a replacement course or a refund of up-front fees.
Imposes obligations on defaulting providers to notify the Tuition Protection Director and students, and on replacement providers to enrol students promptly and not charge for replacement units.
Domestic up-front fee paying students at private higher education providers, and the private providers themselves.

The Education Legislation Amendment (Up-front Payments Tuition Protection) Bill 2020 expands the Tuition Protection Service to cover domestic higher education students who pay upfront, ensuring they receive the same government-backed protection as those with HELP loans. From 1 January 2021, the arrangements will be administered by a statutory director, require private providers to pay annual levies, and include incentive payments for providers taking on displaced students.

The speaker argued in favour of the Education Legislation Amendment (Up-front Payments Tuition Protection) Bill 2020 and the Higher Education (Up-front Payments Tuition Protection Levy) Bill 2020, which extend tuition protection to domestic students who pay upfront fees at private higher education providers, ensuring refunds or course replacements if a provider fails. They also corrected the record that universities were not excluded from JobKeeper, noting that 10% of higher education students (127,000 full-time-equivalent in 2019) study at non-university providers.

The speaker announced Labor would not oppose the bills expanding tuition protection to domestic upfront-fee-paying students, but argued the Morrison government's higher education policies—including $1 billion in annual funding cuts, 12,000 job losses, and fee increases of up to 7% on average—were damaging universities and disadvantaging students.

The member welcomed the bills extending tuition protection to domestic upfront-fee-paying students but criticised the government's higher education funding cuts and fee changes, asserting that 40% of students would pay double their degree costs (an extra $14,500 per year) and that regional universities like Deakin would lose 300 jobs, citing students Lily Watterson and Ana Machado Colling as examples of those affected.

The Education Legislation Amendment (Up-front Payments Tuition Protection) Bill 2020 and related levy bill extend government-backed tuition protection to domestic students who pay fees up-front, ensuring they receive replacement courses or refunds if their provider fails. The levy bill requires viable providers to contribute to a shared fund, reducing individual administrative burdens, with the arrangements taking effect from 2021.
